problems.description: Removing 'LIMIT 50' from get_tasks() makes GET /tasks unbounded, dropping the existing result-set cap with no pagination substitute; fine at story scale but a latent scalability regression that the new test (asserting exactly 55 rows) codifies.

test_list_tasks_ordered_by_created_at_desc inserts three rows in rapid succession; if created_at defaults to second-precision CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (SQLite default), ties make ORDER BY created_at DESC non-deterministic, so the assertion can be flaky.

Measured convention score of 0.70 over-penalizes this commit: 7 of 9 violations live in untouched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py), and the AST shows +0 classes, so the app.py/test_app.py PascalCase flags are pre-existing, not introduced here.

strengths: Substantial test coverage added: 16 functions spanning success and edge cases (missing/blank/no-body title, not-found, empty update) across all four CRUD endpoints.

The 'if updates:' guard in update_task fixes a real defect: an empty payload previously built 'UPDATE tasks SET  WHERE id = ?', which would raise a 500; it now degrades gracefully to returning the task unchanged.
Tests are properly isolated via tempfile DB + monkeypatch + module reload in the fixture, with TESTING config and the test client used correctly.
New code follows existing conventions (snake_case functions, same get_db()/dict access patterns), and no new classes were introduced.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, net-positive Session 1 commit — strong edge-case test coverage and a genuine empty-UPDATE crash fix — but it silently drops the LIMIT 50 result cap and risks a flaky timestamp-ordering test; the 0.70 convention score mostly reflects pre-existing violations in files this commit never touches.

problems.description: login_required mutates the Flask request proxy via `request.user_id = ...` / `request.username = ...`; works in practice but is an unconventional pattern — the idiomatic carrier for per-request auth state is flask.g.

register() does a check-then-insert (TOCTOU): a concurrent duplicate username slips past the get_user_by_username pre-check and the UNIQUE constraint surfaces as an unhandled sqlite3.IntegrityError (500) instead of a 409.
No tests added for the new auth and ownership-scoping paths in the visible diff — register/login/token-expiry and cross-owner task isolation are untested despite the +28 functions.
Single-file app grows by +354 lines; consistent with the existing 'single-file Flask app' design, but auth + JWT + multi-tenancy pushing toward module boundaries in a multi-session story baseline.

Repo-wide convention score is 0.70 with 9 violations, but the visible new code (app.py) is snake_case, type-hinted, and sectioned consistently — most violations sit in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py outside this diff, and the app.py PascalCase/class violation is pre-existing (+0 classes added).

strengths: Ownership scoping is applied uniformly — every read/write path (list, get, update, and the truncated delete) filters by owner_id, so no authz holes are visible.
Solid security hygiene: werkzeug generate/check_password_hash, JWT with 24h expiry, pinned HS256 algorithm, and distinct 400/401/409 responses.
Non-destructive SQLite migration via PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE preserves existing task rows instead of recreating the table.
Faithfully extends the existing single-file architecture — Models/Routes section headers, get_db() context-manager pattern, and jsonify error shapes all match the baseline style.
Type hints on all new public signatures (e.g. create_task(title, owner_id) -> dict) match repo conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped auth + per-user task ownership feature that respects the existing single-file patterns and applies good security hygiene, though it carries minor debt via the request-attribute pattern and an untested TOCTOU in register; convention adherence measures 0.70 but the visible new code is clean, with most violations pre-existing in untouched files.

problems.description: Module-level config attributes in celery_config.py (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes, task_serializer, accept_content, timezone) use snake_case instead of UPPER_CASE per the repo convention (8 of the 9 measured violations).
Legacy users without an email get a silently fabricated default (username@example.com) persisted to the users table, inventing contact data rather than gating the notification on email presence.

The task body is a mock (print/log) and there is no failure surface if no Celery worker is running — the enqueued notification silently never executes. Acceptable for the story, but the enqueue/execute gap is unhandled.

The inline ALTER TABLE migration in init_db mirrors the existing owner_id pattern — consistent with the codebase but unversioned and only applied on app init; the +9 cognitive complexity delta mostly comes from this branch logic.

strengths: Edge-triggered notification (fires only on the status transition to 'completed') is correct and exhaustively tested — retrigger, non-completing updates, and title-only edits all covered.
Clean separation of concerns: app.py only enqueues (.delay, no broker connection at import), task bodies live in celery_tasks.py, and broker/backend are env-overridable in celery_config.py.
The email migration reuses the existing schema-migration pattern already present for owner_id, respecting established codebase structure.
New model helper (get_user_by_id) and tests follow the existing app.py function style and the client/auth_headers test conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, pattern-consistent integration feature (async notifications via Celery/Redis) that cleanly decouples enqueue from execution, though the measured 0.70 convention score reflects snake_case module-level config attributes and a few analyzer flags (e.g. 'Classes should use PascalCase') that don't correspond to visible code, so the practical convention picture is slightly better than the score implies.

problems.description: The refactor inverts part of its own goal: business logic that lived in the deleted model functions (generate_password_hash, the email default, and the created_at timestamp default) was pushed UP into the register/add_task route handlers instead of staying in the repository layer, so encapsulation of data-layer concerns is only partial.

BaseRepository.update and the base get_by_id/build helpers construct SQL columns via f-string interpolation from **fields; table_name is a class constant so it is safe, but column names are caller-supplied kwargs — safe at the current literal call sites, yet a latent SQL-injection vector if ever fed user-derived keys.

Generic BaseRepository.update filters out None-valued fields, meaning a caller can never intentionally set a column to NULL; the None-means-skip semantics are implicit rather than explicit, which is a subtle behavioral contract for future callers.

The measured convention score (0.70, 9 violations) is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, and test_app.py that this commit never touches; only the new repositories.py module-level constant casing is attributable to this diff — the commit's own new code otherwise follows snake_case/PascalCase/type-hint conventions.
SonarQube reports cognitive complexity +1 in the new generic methods; not a bug/smell/duplication but worth monitoring as the base-class SQL builders grow.

strengths: Clean extraction of all SQLite access into a dedicated repository layer, removing ~90 lines of duplicated with get_db() connection handling from app.py and leaving thin, SQL-free route handlers.
Shared BaseRepository(ABC) scaffold with an abstract create plus common get_by_id/update/delete reduces per-table boilerplate (+3 classes, +13 functions, 0 duplication per SonarQube).
No new dependencies: still raw sqlite3 and the existing get_db context-manager pattern, injected as a dependency rather than hard-wired.
Good naming, docstrings, and type hints on all public signatures; consistent with the codebase's existing conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound repository-layer refactor that centralizes SQL access and eliminates duplication (net better), but it leaks password hashing and defaulting logic back into route handlers and builds generic UPDATE columns via f-string interpolation, leaving minor but real architectural debt; the 0.70 convention score largely reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files, not this commit.

problems.description: Cursor pagination orders by `id DESC`, but the pre-existing contract was `ORDER BY created_at DESC` (repositories.py). The implicit ordering change is untested against a case where id and created_at diverge (e.g. backdated inserts) and could surprise consumers relying on created_at ordering.

Rate limiting now hard-depends on Redis at redis://localhost:6379/2 (RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI). The limiter's before_request path will break/block the app if Redis is down or the DB index is flushed by tests, and there is no in-memory fallback for degraded operation.

The blanket `100 per minute` default limit is applied to all endpoints including /auth/register and /auth/login, so per-user credentials attacks are not throttled separately from general traffic and are keyed only by the same shared limiter.
Each page request executes a separate `COUNT(*)` query for `total`, which is fine at this scale but is redundant work for cursor-based clients that only walk pages via next_cursor.

The GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to an envelope ({data, next_cursor, total}) — a breaking client contract change. Acceptable in an in-development app and tests were updated, but the API surface change is unannounced.

strengths: Keyset pagination via `id < cursor` instead of OFFSET — stable and scale-safe ordering of pages.
rate_limit_key decodes the bearer token itself (running ahead of login_required) and falls back to IP when unauthenticated, so the limiter cannot be trivially bypassed by spoofing a user id.
Proper test hygiene: limiter.reset() in the fixture so rate limits don't flake the suite, plus new tests covering default limit, full page walk, and the 55-item case at limit=100.
Parameterized SQL throughout (no injection surface); cursor and limit inputs are validated with clear 400 responses, and a JSON 429 handler preserves the API's error contract.
The change follows the established layering: param validation in the route, the paged query in the TaskRepository, cross-cutting concern (rate limiting) registered as a Flask extension.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested cross-cutting commit that adds keyset pagination and Redis-backed rate limiting while respecting the existing repository/route layering and Flask conventions — the 0.70 convention score is dragged down by violations in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py), so I score the commit's own additions higher and flag the discrepancy.

compounding_issues: The injected naive `datetime.now()` (local-time) timestamp bug survived all five sessions — Session 1 fixed the other two injected bugs but never caught this one, and it propagated untouched through every refactor and feature addition
Session 2's owner_id migration set owner_id=NULL for legacy pre-auth rows, leaving those tasks permanently unreachable once /tasks became owner-scoped (no listing/update path ever touches them)
Build artifacts were committed across sessions 2–5 (__pycache__/*.pyc bytecode grew in every commit) — no .gitignore was ever introduced, so repo hygiene eroded incrementally
key_decisions: Session 1 audited git history, proactively fixed 2 of 3 injected bugs, and built a 14-test pytest harness that became the load-bearing safety net every later session extended
Session 2 added a non-destructive owner_id migration (PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE, preserving existing rows) plus owner-scoped queries, structurally forcing all later sessions to be user-aware
Session 2's JWT login_required decorator became a reusable seam that Session 5's rate limiter reuses (rate_limit_key decodes the token itself to key limits by user)
Session 3 decoupled the email side-effect via Celery, gating the trigger on the actual pending->completed transition to avoid spurious notifications
Session 4 extracted BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository, moving all SQL out of route handlers while keeping get_db/init_db in app.py to honor the do-not-modify-tests constraint
Session 5 replaced list-all with cursor-based keyset pagination ({data, next_cursor, total} envelope) and user-keyed Flask-Limiter rate limiting with IP fallback and 429/Retry-After handling
story_review.trajectory_description: Clear upward arc: the story opened on a minimal 128-line single-file Flask seed carrying three injected bugs; Session 1 stabilized it and built a full test harness (14 tests), and each subsequent session layered one well-scoped concern — JWT auth (32 tests), async Celery notification (38), a pure repository-pattern refactor that preserved identical behavior with untouched tests (38), and rate-limiting plus cursor pagination (51 tests, all passing). The architecture evolved from a monolithic script to a layered one (routes + auth middleware + repository layer + Redis-backed async and rate-limit infrastructure), with the test suite growing monotonically and staying green at every commit. The single persistent blemish is the injected timezone bug, which was never detected and carried quietly through the whole arc.
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental build — CRUD to JWT to async integration to refactor to cross-cutting, every session green and building on the prior, with only the undetected injected timestamp bug marring an otherwise clean upward quality arc.
